newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin suffers new setback in struggle for health.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin suffers new setback in struggle for health.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, forced back into hospital by pneumonia just two months after major heart surgery, found himself fighting a new battle on Thursday to prove he can rule Russia.

The Kremlin, keen to quash alarm over this latest setback, said the 65-year-old president, who was admitted to a Moscow hospital on Wednesday, had a normal temperature and was being treated with antibiotics.

It said Yeltsin had discussed affairs of state by telephone with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and NTV television said arrangements had been made for the Kremlin leader to retain control over Russia's nuclear arsenal from hospital.
Chernomyrdin left Moscow on Thursday for a scheduled break near the capital but was keeping a close eye on developments.
"Treatment of the pneumonia is being carried out with modern antibiotics and with general therapy," a Kremlin statement said.
Heart surgeon Renat Akchurin, who led the quintuple bypass operation on Yeltsin on November 5, said the president's doctors had told him he was in "a quite satisfactory" condition.
Akchurin told reporters the pneumonia was not related to the operation and that the president's overall health allowed him to perform his duties.
"The post-operative period finished a month ago, so it seems to me that it makes no sense to now connect something with the operation," he told reporters.
Yeltsin, who has vast powers under Russia's post-communist constitution, only returned to work on December 23 after almost six months out of the Kremlin with heart problems.
He met German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday -- Yeltsin looked pale and tired during it -- and the Kremlin had built an ambitious schedule of meetings to show he was back in control.

A parliamentary official said on Thursday the first of those meetings, a January 17 summit of the former Soviet states making up the Commonwealth of Independent States might be delayed. It had already been put off from December due to Yeltsin's health.
Alexander Shokhin, a pro-government deputy parliamentary speaker, told RIA news agency Yeltsin had returned to work alarmingly quickly. "There should be no haste here," he said.
Yeltsin's opponents were quick to seize on the illness as a sign he was unable to rule Russia's 150 million people.
"Wherever the president may be...he is not able to take the right decisions," liberal leader Grigory Yavlinsky told Reuters.
General Alexander Lebed, sacked by Yeltsin in October for overt presidential ambitions, went further, telling reporters "there was not much hope" and that Yeltsin should resign.
Russia's fledgling financial markets took the news in their stride. Share prices slid off recent highs but then recovered, and other markets firmed as dealers awaited developments.

But some Russians were sceptical. "First they said he had the flu, now they say it's the first signs of pneumonia. God only knows what he really has," said Alexander Maksutov, 63, a postal worker, interviewed on a snowy central Moscow street.

Kremlin officials announced the new illness quickly after doctors ordered Yeltsin to hospital, but it has not always revealed the full truth about his condition in the past -- notably last summer before Yeltsin announced his heart trouble.
On Monday, aides said the president had a heavy cold after the president cancelled all appointments from Monday and moved to a residence outside Moscow to rest.
On Wednesday evening, it said doctors had detected early signs of pneumonia when they examined the Kremlin leader and had decided to transfer him to Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital.
A presidential spokesman said Yeltsin entered the hospital at about nine p.m. (1800 GMT) on Wednesday.
Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey who advised Akchurin over Yeltsin's heart surgery, joined his Russian colleagues in ruling out a link with the operation.
Asked if Yeltsin had recovered from the trauma of the heart surgery, DeBakey said: "I would say pretty much yes and his heart is functioning now virtually normally."

Yeltsin suffered two heart attacks in 1995 and his long absences from the Kremlin fuelled a struggle for position among Kremlin officials. Chernomyrdin took on extra powers but only assumed formal control for a day during the operation itself.

If Yeltsin, who has played a major role in Russia's transition from communist rule and has been president since 1991, was unable to govern, Chernomyrdin would stand in for up to three months before an election.

On his return to the Kremlin, Yeltsin vowed to deal with problems which had built up in his absence, including tax evasion which drained state coffers and led to long delays in wage and pension payments. But he has not had time to do so.
